types.name: FConfigIniStruct
types.doc:
UE's struct spelling inside a value: (Name="Jump",Type=Button,Keys=("A","B")).
Fields split at top-level commas — parentheses nest, quotes hide commas — and
keep their quotes until Unquote, so a reader can tell the text "1" from 1.

FromNode/ToNode carry an MDF node through it losslessly: Name= is the node's
name, each property keeps its key (a list as (a,b), text always quoted), and
each child type is a capitalised key holding a list of child structs —
(Name="Jump",type="Button",Binding=((Name="Key",key="Space"))). Properties are
lower-case and child types capitalised in every MDF config this replaces, so
the case of the key is what tells them apart.

types.name: FConfigClassBinder
types.doc:
`[/Script/<Module>.<Class>]` onto a reflected object. The section names the
class without its M/A prefix the way UE drops U/A ("/Script/Mowo.HealthComponent"
for MHealthComponent); the module part is not checked, since an MClass does
not know its module. Super-class sections apply first, so a subclass section
overrides its base. Each key sets the MPROPERTY(Config) of that name — a
field without the flag is never written, whatever the file says: bool,
integers, float, double, std::string, std::vector<std::string> (from a list).

UE's MCLASS(Config=Game) picks the one file a class reads; here a class is a
config class when any field up its chain is MPROPERTY(Config), and the caller
applies Engine then Game, so a Game section wins. MCLASS(Config=Game) is kept
on the MClass (FMClassFlags::Config and the "Config" meta entry), but the
binder does not narrow the files by it: the section name already decides
which keys apply.

members.name: RestrictToPlayerArguments
members.doc:
Drops every argument a shipped game has no business honouring and logs
what it dropped. Called once by the game host right after Set(); the
editor, the tests and the server never call it.

A packaged game's command line is user-editable — a shortcut, a Steam
launch option, a batch file someone found online — and everything in the
engine reads from here: `--cvar=` reaches every console variable,
`--scene` loads any file on disk, the self-test and profiling switches
start machinery a player should never be inside. Keeping the parse and
filtering the RESULT (rather than teaching each reader to re-check) is
what makes the guarantee hold for code that has not been written yet.

What survives is the player-facing set: the graphics backend shorthands,
window/display, audio, language, the multiplayer join arguments and the
save slot. `allowExtra` lets a game module widen it with its own
switches (no leading dashes, no values). Returns what it dropped, in
argv order, for the caller to log — Core sits below Logging.

members.name: FUnloadHandler
members.doc:
Module-unload broadcast: fired from UnloadModule after the module's
own ShutdownModule hook and BEFORE the image is freed, so a handler
can still touch code and data inside the dying module. This is how
the additive registries (scene systems, reflection descriptors,
online services, asset validators, net-session providers) drop
function pointers that would otherwise keep pointing into freed
pages. Handlers are process-lifetime plain function pointers from
never-unloaded engine modules; duplicates are ignored.

members.name: FModuleVerifier
members.signature: using FModuleVerifier = bool (*)(const std::string& resolvedPath, void* image, std::string& outReason)
members.doc:
Verify-before-load gate. The ABI check in LoadModuleFromPath only runs
AFTER LoadLibrary has already executed the image's static init (DllMain),
so a hostile or wrong module gets to run code before it is (maybe)
refused. A higher tier — one that can reach the EdDSA/hash crypto in
Filesystem — registers a verifier here; the loader calls it on the
resolved binary PATH *before* the image is mapped, and a false result
refuses the load with the image never touched. With no verifier
registered the loader behaves exactly as before (unsigned local/dev
modules load), so this is opt-in hardening a shipping host arms. One
verifier, process-lifetime; the last registration wins. `outReason` is
logged on refusal.

`image` is the IPlatformLibrary::OpenImageForLoad handle the loader holds
from before the verifier runs until after the image is mapped: the
verifier reads the bytes through it (IPlatformLibrary::ReadImage), so
what it vouches for is what gets mapped. The module's imports that are
files the game ships, not yet mapped, are held and verified the same way
before the load — an unsigned DLL beside a signed plugin would otherwise
come in as its dependency, without ever passing the gate.

The process-wide frame clock: one real time that never stretches, one
game time that does, and the frame number everything else keys off.

Every accessor is out-of-line and the state lives in exactly one
translation unit inside Core.dll. Nothing here may become an inline
member reading a header-declared static — that shape gives each

about what frame it is without anything failing loudly.

types.name: ECVarSetBy
types.doc:

members.signature: static EPluralCategory PluralCategory(const std::string& locale, int64_t count)
members.doc:
CLDR cardinal category of `count` under `locale`'s rules (integer
counts only — game quantities are integers). Region subtags are
ignored ("ru-RU" → "ru"); unknown languages use the English rule, so
a new locale degrades to two forms instead of crashing or pluralizing
Russian with an English rule silently — the table fallback below still
finds `.other`.

The rules are CLDR's cardinal rules for integers, generated by hand from
plurals.xml: en de nl sv da nb fi et it es ca gl el hu tr bg ka (one/other),
fr and pt-BR (0 and 1 are one; fr has many for exact millions), pt-PT,
hi bn gu kn mr fa (0 and 1 are one), ru uk be, pl, cs sk, hr sr bs, lt,
lv, ro, he, sl, mk, ar, cy, ga, and the no-plural group
ja zh ko vi th id ms lo my km.

the count, so callers write one line:

Returns true on insert; false for nullptr or a duplicate typeid

members.name: RegisterNamed
members.doc:
Data-driven classes have no C++ type, so no std::type_index to key
on — Visual Script builds an MClass at runtime from a .vscript asset and registers
it BY NAME here so SpawnActorByClass / FindByName resolve it like any
codegen class. The registry does NOT own the MClass (the caller, e.g.

members.name: UnregisterAllInModule
members.doc:
Drop every MClass whose static instance lives inside the given
module binary (handle from FModuleManager::GetModuleHandle).
Attribution is by ADDRESS — generated MClass instances are
statics in the module's .refl.cpp TUs, so their addresses fall
inside the module image. Call BEFORE the library is freed.
Also clears cached superClass links pointing into the dropped
set (other modules' classes may have lazily linked to them).
Returns the number of classes dropped.

types.name: FMPropertyValueOps
types.doc:
What the kind alone cannot say about an MPROPERTY field: whether its BYTES
are its whole value, and — for a std::vector field — how to walk and resize
it without naming the element type. Both answers come from the C++ compiler
at codegen time and cannot be recovered from the type's spelling, which is
why they travel with the property row.

`triviallyCopyable` is the same line MREPLICATED draws: a Struct or Custom
field whose bytes hide a heap pointer must not be copied verbatim into
storage that outlives the object, so a consumer that stores raw bytes
checks this first. It does NOT promise the bytes are meaningful in another
process or after the referent dies — a POD struct holding a raw pointer
passes the trait and still restores a stale address; mark those
MOWO_RUNTIME_ONLY.

types.name: TObjectPtr
types.doc:
UE's TObjectPtr: behaves like a plain T* in every read, but every
STORE shades the new referent through the incremental GC's write
barrier — a mid-mark assignment can no longer hide a white object
behind an already-black owner. It does NOT root; reachability comes from
the owner's MPROPERTY trace, exactly like a raw pointer. A traced one whose
target is destroyed (pending kill) is nulled by the next mark, before the
sweep frees the target; an untraced one (a local, a member that is not an
MPROPERTY) is not, which is what TWeakObjectPtr is for.

The incremental GC (`mowo.GC.Incremental`) is only sound over object
graphs whose MPROPERTY edges are barriered — migrate a class's raw
MPROPERTY pointers to TObjectPtr before budget-marking worlds built
from it. Codegen needs no changes: the CollectReference overload set
traces it, and sizeof(TObjectPtr<T>) == sizeof(T*).

types.name: TStrongObjectPtr
types.doc:
Owning handle that adds its referent to FMObjectArray's root set, so the GC
can't sweep it out from under us. Use when a non-MObject holder needs to
keep an MObject alive without being its Outer; an MObject reached through
the Outer chain or an MPROPERTY needs no explicit root. Copyable: the root
set counts, so every copy is one more owner and the object stays rooted
until the last one lets go — including an owner that rooted it by hand.

Destroy still wins (a pending-kill root is collected, as it always was).
The handle remembers the slot's serial, so after that sweep Get() answers
null and letting go touches nothing, instead of reading freed memory.

T must derive from RefCounted (our assets are intrusive-refcounted,
not MObjects — asset lifetime stays with the Ref system, NOT the GC).

types.name: WeakRef
types.doc:
WeakRef<T> — non-owning reference to a RefCounted object. Does not keep
the object alive; Lock() promotes to a Ref when it is still there.

The observation lives in the object's FWeakRefControl, which outlives the
object, so every operation here is safe after the last strong ref is gone.
